title: The Prompt Ladder
tagline: Teachers climb eight rungs of prompts for the same classroom task, predict each mock AI output before reading it, and weigh what every added detail gains and what it costs.
groupSize: Teams of 3–4; any number of teams
overview: A chatbot predicts its answer from patterns it learned plus the words you give it, so your prompt is the context it predicts from. Adding detail usually narrows the output toward what you want, but not always for free. In this unplugged session, teams climb a "ladder" of eight prompts for one real teacher task (a 4th-grade water-cycle exit ticket). At each rung, they predict what the AI will produce, read a printed mock output, and score the tradeoff. Two rungs are traps: one where a prompt's built-in misconception gets repeated back as fact, and one that works well but pastes private student information into the tool. Teachers leave with a prompting habit they can model for students: add the context that serves the learning, and stop before it costs accuracy or privacy.
objectives: Participants will explain why added context changes a chatbot's output, using the idea that the model predicts from patterns plus the prompt.
Participants will evaluate prompting tradeoffs: quality gained versus time spent, loss of variety, steering the output toward the prompter's assumptions, and privacy risk.
Participants will rewrite an over-sharing prompt so it keeps the instructional benefit without any identifying student information.
Participants will draft a three-rung prompt ladder for a real task and decide where to stop, or whether AI is needed at all.

print: Handout A: Prompt Rung Cards (1 set per team, cut apart and stacked in order, face down; backs printed as a facilitator key)
Handout B: Mock Outputs (1 per team, folded or kept face down until each prediction is made)
Handout C: Prompt Tradeoff Scorecard (1 per team)
digital: Optional: a generative AI chatbot your district approves, projected by the facilitator only, to run rungs 1, 3, and 5 live
Optional: a shared document per team for the Transfer ladder

prep: Print and cut Handout A; stack the cards in rung order. Print Handout B so each output can be revealed one at a time (fold it accordion-style or cut the outputs apart).

Read the facilitator key on the card backs, especially Rung 5 (the misconception: clouds are made of tiny liquid water droplets or ice crystals, not water vapor, which is invisible) and Rung 6 (private student information).
Check your district's guidance on what may be entered into AI tools. Have it on a slide for the Model step.

steps.title: More words, narrower guesses
steps.body: Ask the room to finish each phrase aloud as you add words: "The…" (anything goes). "The water…" "The water in the puddle…" "On a hot, sunny afternoon, the water in the puddle…" (*dried up, evaporated*). Say: "Every word I added narrowed your prediction. A chatbot does something similar: it predicts its answer from patterns it learned plus everything in your prompt. Your prompt is its context. Today we test when more context helps, and when it costs something."
steps.note: If people ask how the prediction works under the hood, save it for a follow-up session. Keep the focus on the prompt as context.

steps.title: Play the chatbot
steps.body: One person on each team is the "chatbot." Flip Rung 1 ("water cycle questions"). The chatbot has 60 seconds to write the questions they'd produce, with no follow-up questions allowed, because a chatbot answers what it's given. Teammates then read Output 1 on Handout B and compare. Ask: "What did the chatbot have to *guess*? Grade level? How many? What kind of thinking?" Log Rung 1 on Handout C.
steps.note: Human "chatbots" usually make the same guesses as the mock output: generic recall questions at a mixed level. That's the point: vague prompts force guessing, and the guess is the most common pattern.

steps.title: Climb the ladder
steps.body: Teams flip Rungs 2–8 one at a time. For each rung: **predict** in one sentence what will change in the output, **read** the matching output on Handout B, then **score** the rung on Handout C: what improved, what it cost (time, variety, steering, privacy), and whether it was worth it. Rotate the reader for each rung.
steps.note: Watch Rung 5. Some teams won't notice that the output repeats the prompt's misconception (clouds as water vapor). If they miss it, ask: "Is every answer in the key correct?"

steps.title: The two traps, out loud
steps.body: Think aloud about **Rung 5**: "My prompt assumed clouds are water vapor. The output built an answer key on my mistake and marked it *true*. A more specific prompt made the output worse because my specifics were wrong. The model tends to follow the framing I give it." Then **Rung 6**: "This output is genuinely useful. And I just typed two students' names, disability plans, and quiz failures into a tool. Watch me rewrite it." Write on chart paper: *"Make one version with shorter sentences and a word bank, and one with three questions instead of five, including one drawing question."* Same instructional benefit, no identifying information. Show the district's guidance slide.
steps.note: Emerging-tech angle (Teacher ELE 1.3): many tools now add memory, file uploads, and saved custom instructions, which means more context travels with every prompt. The privacy question gets bigger, not smaller.

steps.title: Where would you stop climbing?
steps.body: Each team puts a sticky note on the rung where they'd stop for this task and says why. Discuss: "Which rung gave the biggest jump in quality for the least effort?" (Usually Rung 3: stating the evidence of learning you want.) "Which rungs made the output worse or riskier?" "Would writing these five questions yourself have been faster?" For some teachers, it would, and that's a legitimate answer.
steps.note: Connect to the 2026 ELE question: the best prompt is the one that states the *evidence of learning* you want. Rung 3 is Evidence Before Tools in prompt form.

steps.title: Your own three rungs
steps.body: On the back of Handout C, each person writes a three-rung ladder for a real upcoming task: a vague prompt, a prompt that states the audience and the evidence of learning, and a prompt that adds one helpful constraint. Beside it, they write one thing they'll never put in a prompt and one sign that they should stop prompting and just write it themselves. Then plan how you'd run a student version: students climb a ladder for their own study task and explain which rung helped their learning.
steps.note: For students under 13, the teacher runs any live prompts on a projector; the ladder itself works on paper at any age.

unplugged: The session is designed to run unplugged: prompts are cards, outputs are printed, and the human "chatbot" in Explore makes the prediction idea concrete. Printed mock outputs also guarantee every team sees the same results, which live tools can't.
digital: After the Practice step, the facilitator runs Rungs 1, 3, and 5 live in a district-approved chatbot on the projector. Participants compare the real outputs with the mock ones: Does the real tool repeat the cloud misconception or correct it? Results vary by tool and day, and that variation is itself a lesson. Never demonstrate Rung 6 with real names; if you show it, use the rewritten version. In a virtual session, share the cards and outputs as slides revealed one at a time, with a shared scorecard per breakout room.
whyTech: Running three rungs live lets teachers check the paper claims against a real tool and see that outputs vary, and that some tools correct a wrong premise while others repeat it. The ladder itself is better on paper, because fixed outputs keep the discussion on the tradeoffs rather than on whatever the tool happened to say today.

adaptations.label: K–2 teachers
adaptations.text: Use Rungs 1, 2, 3, and 6 with a K–2 task (for example, a read-aloud discussion question). The student version becomes a teacher-led talk: "What did I need to tell the computer so it could help us?"

adaptations.label: Secondary teachers
adaptations.text: Have students build a ladder for a study task (a practice quiz, a counterargument, feedback on a draft), then submit their best prompt with a one-sentence justification and a note on what they checked in the output.

adaptations.label: Librarians
adaptations.text: Compare the ladder with search-query refinement: what carries over from database searching (specificity, limiters) and what doesn't (a chatbot will answer even when its sources are thin).

adaptations.label: Higher Ed faculty
adaptations.text: Swap the task for a course-level one (a case-study prompt, a rubric draft) and add a rung that asks the model to cite sources, then check whether the citations exist.

lookFors: Handout C predictions become more accurate as teams climb, showing they understand the prompt as context for prediction.
Teams catch the Rung 5 misconception and explain that a prompt's wrong assumption can be repeated back as fact.
Participants rewrite Rung 6 so it keeps the differentiation benefit with no names, plans, or other identifying details.
Transfer ladders include a rung that states the evidence of learning, plus a stated "stop and write it myself" signal.
reflection: How can I use AI tools to enhance student learning while modeling careful, ethical prompting for students? (Teacher ELE 1.2)
Which details about my students help an AI tool without identifying anyone, and which should never leave my classroom?
As AI tools add memory and file uploads, what new questions do I need to ask before using them? (Teacher ELE 1.3)
transfer: Use your three-rung ladder for a real task this week and keep the outputs. Then teach students one ladder climb for a study task, and collect their best prompt plus a sentence explaining which rung improved their learning and what they checked in the output.

handouts.title: Prompt Rung Cards
handouts.instructions: Stack in order, face down. Flip one rung at a time, predict the output, then read it on Handout B. Card backs are the facilitator key: print them separately. Student names are fictional.

cards.label: Rung 1 · Vague
cards.back: The model must guess grade, number, format, and purpose, so it produces the most common pattern: generic recall at mixed levels. Cost: little effort now, lots of editing later.

cards.label: Rung 2 · Task + audience
cards.front: "Write a 5-question exit ticket on the water cycle for 4th graders."
cards.back: Big jump for a few words: the right length and level. Still mostly recall, because the prompt didn't say what kind of thinking to show.

cards.label: Rung 3 · + Evidence of learning
cards.front: Rung 2, plus: "I want to see whether students can explain how water moves between stages, not just name the stages. At least two questions should ask students to explain why."
cards.back: Usually the best value on the ladder: stating the evidence you want changes the kind of questions, not just their wording. Evidence Before Tools, in prompt form.

cards.label: Rung 4 · + Learners
cards.front: Rung 3, plus: "Many of my students are learning English. Use short sentences, bold the key vocabulary, and include one question students can answer with a labeled drawing."
cards.back: Describing needs, not individuals, adds access with no privacy cost. Tradeoff: the teacher still has to check that simplified wording didn't change the science.

cards.label: Rung 5 · Trap: steering
cards.front: "Write 5 exit-ticket questions for 4th graders that check whether they understand that clouds are made of water vapor."
cards.back: The prompt carries a misconception: clouds are tiny liquid water droplets or ice crystals, and water vapor is an invisible gas. The output builds its key on the mistake. Specific isn't the same as correct; the model tends to follow the framing you give it.

cards.label: Rung 6 · Trap: over-sharing
cards.front: "These students failed the last quiz: Maria G. (IEP, reading accommodations) and Devon T. (504 plan, ADHD). Make a personalized version of the exit ticket for each of them."
cards.back: The output is useful, and the prompt put names, disability plans, and grades into a tool. Rewrite: "Make one version with shorter sentences and a word bank, and one with three questions instead of five, including one drawing question." Same benefit, no identifying information. Follow district guidance.

cards.label: Rung 7 · Example
cards.front: Rung 4, plus: "Here is a question I like: 'Why does a puddle get smaller on a sunny day? Use the word evaporation.' Write four more like it."
cards.back: An example matches your style well. Tradeoff: variety drops, and the model copies your example's pattern, including any weakness (every question now uses a 'Use the word ___' frame).

cards.label: Rung 8 · Follow-up
cards.front: A second message after Rung 4's output: "Question 3 is too easy. Change it so students have to compare two stages of the water cycle."
cards.back: Iterating targets one flaw without starting over. Cost: time, and each new version still needs checking. Ask yourself: would writing it myself be faster now?

handouts.title: Mock Outputs
handouts.instructions: Fictional outputs written for this activity. Reveal each one only after your team writes its prediction for that rung.
paragraphs: **Output 1:** "Here are some water cycle questions! 1. What is the water cycle? 2. What is evaporation? 3. What is condensation? 4. What is precipitation? 5. What is transpiration? 6. What is sublimation? 7. Name the four stages of the water cycle. 8. Where does rain come from? 9. What powers the water cycle? 10. Why is the water cycle important? Let me know if you'd like an answer key!"

**Output 2:** "4th Grade Exit Ticket: The Water Cycle. 1. What is evaporation? 2. What is condensation? 3. Rain, snow, sleet, and hail are all kinds of ______. 4. What gives the water cycle its energy? 5. Name one place where water collects after it falls."

**Output 3:** "1. A puddle is gone after a sunny afternoon. Explain where the water went. 2. Why do drops of water form on the outside of a cold glass on a hot day? 3. What has to happen to water vapor in the air before it can fall as rain? 4. Explain why the Sun is important to the water cycle. 5. Choose two stages of the water cycle and explain how one leads to the other."

**Output 4:** "1. The Sun heats a puddle. Where does the water go? Use the word **evaporation**. 2. A cold glass gets wet on the outside. Why? Use the word **condensation**. 3. What must happen in a cloud before rain falls? 4. Why does the water cycle need the Sun? 5. Draw the water cycle. Label **evaporation**, **condensation**, **precipitation**, and **collection**. Word bank: evaporation, condensation, precipitation, collection, water vapor."

**Output 5:** "1. True or false: Clouds are made of water vapor. (Answer: True) 2. What happens when water vapor rises into the sky? (Answer: It forms clouds made of water vapor.) 3. Fill in the blank: Clouds are made of ______. (Answer: water vapor) 4. Why can we see clouds? (Answer: Because the water vapor gathers together.) 5. Draw a cloud and label the water vapor inside it."

**Output 6:** "Version for Maria G. (reading accommodations): 1. The Sun heats water. Where does it go? 2. A cold glass gets wet. Why? 3. Draw rain falling from a cloud. — Version for Devon T. (ADHD): three short questions with a check box after each, and a movement break after question 2. Tip: keep Devon's version on one page so it feels manageable!"

**Output 7:** "1. Why does a wet towel dry on a clothesline? Use the word evaporation. 2. Why do drops form on a bathroom mirror after a hot shower? Use the word condensation. 3. Why does rain fall from clouds? Use the word precipitation. 4. Where does rainwater go after it falls? Use the word collection."
**Output 8:** "Here's a revised Question 3: Compare **evaporation** and **condensation**. How are they opposites? Give one example of each that you might see at home."

handouts.title: Prompt Tradeoff Scorecard
handouts.instructions: Before reading each output, write your prediction. Costs to consider: time · lost variety · steering (the prompt's assumptions) · privacy.
